name: Memento
intent: Capture an object's internal state in a snapshot so it can be restored later, without exposing its internals.
scenario: A game saves checkpoints of the player's health and level, and can load the last one after a bad fight.
problem: To save and restore a player the save code needs to read every field and write them back. That forces the player to expose its internals publicly, and any new field means updating the save code too.
solution: The player (the originator) creates a Snapshot object of its own state and can restore itself from one. The snapshot is opaque to everyone else. A CheckpointManager (the caretaker) only stores snapshots in a stack and hands them back. It never looks inside.
pain: The save code reads and writes the player's fields directly
Adding a field means updating the save code, or saves silently lose data
Any code can corrupt the player by poking its fields
benefits: The player keeps its fields private
Snapshots are created and restored by the player itself
Adding a field changes only the player and its snapshot
The caretaker stores snapshots without knowing their contents
whenToUse: You need undo, checkpoints, or rollback
Direct access to an object's fields would break its encapsulation
State snapshots should be immutable and opaque
whenNotToUse: The state is huge and snapshots would use too much memory
Objects hold things that cannot be snapshotted (open connections)
A simple copy or the Command pattern's undo is enough
pitfalls: Memory: many snapshots of large state add up fast
The caretaker may keep stale snapshots forever
Snapshots of objects with references need deep copies
Easy to confuse with Command undo: Memento restores saved state, Command reverses an action

roles.label: Originator
roles.description: Creates snapshots of itself and restores from them.

roles.label: Memento
roles.description: Immutable, opaque snapshot of the originator's state.

quiz.question: A game saves a player by reading the player's public fields from outside and writing them back on load. A shield field is added to the player and nobody updates the save code, so loaded players lose their shield. What is the best design?
options: Have the player create and restore its own opaque snapshot
Make the save code use reflection on the player so that new fields are found automatically
Add a unit test that fails when the player has a field the save code does not read
Make every field of the player public so that the save code can reach each one
quiz.explanation: The object that owns the state knows all of it, so it should create and restore the snapshot, and no outside code needs its fields. Reflection or public fields still break encapsulation, and a test only detects the problem after it was introduced.

quiz.question: A checkpoint snapshot of a player stores a reference to the player's inventory list instead of a copy. After loading a checkpoint, items picked up after the save are still in the inventory. What is the cause and the fix?
options: The snapshot is not immutable, so it should be stored in a read-only file on disk
The snapshot shares the live list, so it needs a deep copy of the inventory when it is created
The manager keeps stale snapshots too long, so it should delete a snapshot as soon as it is loaded
The restore runs before the inventory exists, so it should run after the game scene loads
quiz.explanation: A snapshot that holds a reference sees later changes made to the same list, so it did not capture the past. Copying the contents when the snapshot is taken fixes this. Deleting snapshots does not change what they hold.

quiz.question: A spreadsheet has 1 million cells. Each user action changes one cell, and the app keeps 200 levels of undo. Taking a full snapshot per action costs about 200 times the sheet size. What is the best approach?
options: Keep full snapshots but cap undo at 5 levels, which keeps memory small and rarely matters
Keep full snapshots but write them to disk, since disk is cheaper than memory
Record only the changed cell and its old value, and undo by restoring it
Keep full snapshots but compress them, since gzip reduces repeated cell data very well
quiz.explanation: When the state is huge and each action touches little, storing the change is far smaller than storing everything. Memento fits small state or infrequent saves. Compression, disk and a lower cap only reduce a cost that is the wrong size to begin with.
